title: A Ruined Land, a New Heart
overview: God promises the exiles that their ruined, mocked homeland will flourish again and that he will cleanse them and give them a new heart, not because they earned it but to restore the honor of his name.

parts.label: Words to the empty land (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: With the people carried off to Babylon, Ezekiel speaks to the land itself, which neighbors, especially Edom, had seized and laughed at. Raising a hand was how people swore an oath, and God swears the mockers will one day bear shame themselves.

parts.label: The hills will bloom again (vv. 8-15)
parts.note: The hills will be farmed and the towns rebuilt because the exiles are coming home soon, most likely pointing to the return from Babylon decades later. People said the land 'devours' its own people, remembering war and famine there, but it will stop being a place of loss.

parts.label: Why the exile happened (vv. 16-23)
parts.note: Violence and idol worship had made the land unclean, which the text compares to the old purity laws that kept a menstruating woman apart from worship for a time. Scattered abroad, the people made the LORD look powerless, so he will act not because they deserve it but to restore the honor of his name.

parts.label: Clean water, a new heart (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: Sprinkling water echoes cleansing rites in Israel's law, and a heart of stone is a will that no longer responds, while a heart of flesh can feel and respond. God promises to put his own Spirit in them; Christians have often read this as pointing to the new life they believe God gives through Jesus.

parts.label: Home, harvest and regret (vv. 28-32)
parts.note: They will live in the land as God's people again, with harvests good enough that famine no longer shames them. Kindness they did not earn will make them look back on their past with deep regret, and God repeats that this is not a reward.

parts.label: Like the garden of Eden (vv. 33-38)
parts.note: Passersby who saw only ruins will say the land now looks like Eden, and the surrounding nations will recognize the LORD's work. At festivals Jerusalem filled with flocks of sheep brought for sacrifice, and the empty towns will be just as crowded with people.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether this promise of return and renewal was fulfilled in the return from Babylon and spiritually in the church, or still points to a future restoration of the Jewish people to their land.
think: What do you think actually changes a person deep down: their own effort, their circumstances, or something that has to come from outside them?
